column5: Guiding the redeemed by strength
column6: In the Song at the Sea, YHWH leads the people he redeemed and guides them by his strength to his holy dwelling; it joins rescue, help, and a destination on the journey the commentary asks God to guide.

column5: A perilous wilderness journey
column6: Moses recalls YHWH leading Israel through a great, dangerous wilderness and bringing water from flint; the community's physical dependence on guidance and sustenance closely expands the commentary's tired traveler.

column5: The guide goes before and does not abandon
column6: Moses tells Joshua that YHWH goes before him and will not fail or forsake him; it makes the sought guidance personal and reassuring for someone unable to proceed alone.

column5: Feet sustained through forty years
column6: In a communal confession, the people say God sustained them in the wilderness for forty years, their clothes did not wear out and their feet did not swell; it makes divine aid concrete in the body of travelers.

column5: Feet made like a deer's
column6: YHWH makes the speaker's feet like a deer's and sets him on secure heights; it pictures strength and stable footing after the commentary's image of a halted, unsteady traveler.

column5: A broad place for each step
column6: The speaker says God enlarged the place beneath his steps so his feet did not slip; this gives a direct image of supported walking and secure footing.

column5: A level place for worship
column6: The speaker says his foot stands on level ground and blesses YHWH in the assembly; it joins stable posture with worship, two elements the commentary brings together in the needy traveler's prayer.

column5: Kept from slipping
column6: The psalm says God keeps the community alive and does not let its feet slip; this is a specific image of ongoing support for people who could otherwise fall.

column5: A flock led by two human guides
column6: The psalm says God led his people like a flock by the hand of Moses and Aaron; divine guidance is mediated through two human leaders, adding a communal counterpart to the commentary's walker leaning between two people.

column5: Feet saved from stumbling
column6: The speaker says YHWH rescued his soul from death, his eyes from tears, and his feet from stumbling; the last detail explicitly links divine rescue to continued walking.

column5: A level path for the righteous
column6: The prophet says the path of the righteous is level and God makes it smooth; this sharpens the commentary's image of guidance into a road made passable for the walker.

column5: Direction when turning right or left
column6: The people hear a voice behind them saying, “This is the way; walk in it,” when they turn right or left; it uniquely connects guidance with the commentary's side-to-side swaying walker.

column5: A safe highway for the redeemed
column6: Isaiah continues the restoration scene with a highway called the holy way, on which even the travelers will not stray; it supplies the safe, morally directed road that follows the weak hands and knees in the same chapter.

column5: The shepherd carries and gently leads
column6: YHWH gathers lambs in his arm, carries them close, and gently leads those with young; the verse gives a concrete image of help adjusted to a traveler's weakness.

column5: Upheld by God's hand
column6: YHWH tells fearful Israel not to fear, promises help, and says he will uphold them with his righteous hand; the bodily act of holding someone up closely matches the commentary's dependent walker.

column5: A word that sustains the weary
column6: The servant says God gives him a trained tongue to sustain the weary with a word; this adds speech as support alongside the commentary's shoulders, upright body, and calm gait.

column5: God makes the path straight
column6: The proverb says to acknowledge YHWH in all one's ways and he will make the paths straight; this is a direct formulation of asking God to guide one along a straight way.

column5: Walking securely without stumbling
column6: The pupil will walk securely and his foot will not stumble; this states the bodily result of the steady path and support developed in the commentary.

column5: Confidence that keeps the foot
column6: YHWH is the pupil's confidence and keeps his foot from being caught; the verse makes divine reliance a protection for the body's movement.

column5: Make the path level for your feet
column6: The wisdom teacher tells the pupil to make a level path for his feet and make all his ways sure; this continues the same chapter's taught walk with an explicit act of stabilizing the road.

column5: Do not turn aside
column6: The pupil is told not to swerve right or left but to turn his foot away from evil; this adds a moral direction to the commentary's image of swaying from side to side.

column5: A lifted yoke and food for the dependent
column6: YHWH describes leading Ephraim with human kindness, lifting the yoke from its jaws, and bending down to feed it; it adds gentle, practical care for a dependent being to the commentary's exhausted mount and traveler.

column5: Worship with a textual variant about support
column6: WLC's ketiv vocalizes the final noun as “bed,” while its qere reads “staff”; only the qere makes Jacob's worship explicitly lean on a support, so this verse should preserve the distinction rather than silently treating the staff as WLC's written reading.

column5: Jacob worships leaning on his staff
column6: Hebrews recounts Jacob blessing Joseph's sons and worshiping while leaning on his staff, following the Greek reading of Genesis 47:31; it makes worship and physical support occur together, exactly the pairing developed in the commentary.

column5: A sinking walker cries for help
column6: Peter begins to sink while walking on the water and cries, “Lord, save me”; this is a precise scene of someone whose movement fails and who asks another for immediate aid.

column5: A hand catches the failing walker
column6: Jesus immediately reaches out and catches Peter; the physical rescue answers the cry for help and supplies the hand support missing from the commentary's faltering traveler.

column5: A roadside traveler asks for mercy
column6: Near Jericho, the blind man Bartimaeus cries to Jesus for mercy as Jesus passes; his vulnerable position on the road and direct plea for help make the need for assistance concrete.

column5: Restored sight and a guided way
column6: The healed man follows Jesus on the way, glorifying God; it joins recovery of a dependent person, continued movement, and worship as the commentary does.

column5: Friends carry a man who cannot walk
column6: Four people bring a paralyzed man to Jesus on a mat; their coordinated carrying makes the commentary's reliance on other bodies literal and communal.

column5: The Spirit helps weakness in prayer
column6: Paul says the Spirit helps believers in their weakness because they do not know how to pray as they ought; this closely links the commentary's inability to proceed alone with its joining worship and a request for help.

column5: Kept from stumbling and presented standing
column6: The doxology praises God as able to keep believers from stumbling and present them blameless before his glory; it turns the commentary's bodily image of being steadied into a promise about standing securely before God.

column5: The nations gathered and separated
column6: Jesus continues the throne scene by gathering all nations and separating them; this supplies the judgment action following the royal appearance in the preceding verse of the same passage.

column5: Do not rely on your own understanding
column6: The proverb tells the pupil not to lean on his own understanding but to trust YHWH; this makes dependence explicit beside the commentary's image of a traveler who cannot support himself, though the proverb speaks metaphorically.

column5: A reader asks for someone to guide him
column6: The Ethiopian official says he cannot understand Isaiah unless someone guides him; this shifts the commentary's dependent traveler's need for guidance to interpretation, showing why a guide may be needed even by a capable traveler.

column5: A companion joins travelers on the road
column6: As two disciples walk sadly toward Emmaus, Jesus draws near and walks with them; this echoes the commentary's image of a vulnerable walk made in company, though the aid is companionship rather than physical support.

column5: A guide interprets the road's meaning
column6: Jesus interprets Moses and the prophets to the two travelers; this adds scriptural instruction to the commentary's image of a guide who helps a dependent person find the way.

column5: The Lord is the helper
column6: The author quotes the confession that the Lord is one's helper and therefore one need not fear; it gives a direct first-person expression of reliance, though it does not develop the travel image.

column5: Aid for whoever asks
column6: The Didache instructs its hearer to give to everyone who asks; within its teaching on the way of life, it makes the commentary's image of receiving support into a concrete obligation to support others.
